papers.title: Entering and Exiting Awareness are Asymmetrical: Evidence from tracking Continuous Flash Suppression
papers.abstract: This study provides a model for obtaining cleaner threshold estimates of entry into and exit from conscious awareness measured with the popular breaking continuous flash suppression (bCFS) and newer tracking CFS (tCFS) paradigms. In both, a suppressed target increases in contrast until it breaks into awareness. tCFS also measures exit thresholds by reversing the contrast change. Both CFS paradigms require a response when the threshold is reached and thus involve a reaction-time component. During this period, target contrast continues to change and threshold estimates are inflated (the "overshoot" problem). Here, we measure reaction-time components for both increasing (entering awareness) and decreasing targets (exiting awareness). We find overshoot is asymmetrical, being greater for stimuli entering (breakthrough thresholds) than for exiting awareness (suppression thresholds). To solve "the overshoot problem", we introduce a mathematical model that quantifies reaction-time components so they can be partialled out to produce clean breakthrough and suppression thresholds. The model can also be applied to previously published CFS studies. The model works for simple target detection and two-alternative target discrimination, even in the continuous tracking paradigm of tCFS. With the timing corrections applied, changes in pupil diameter around transitions in awareness are shown to align with the corrected time points, most clearly when targets exit awareness. Even after correction, the contrast decrease required for a target to exit awareness was greater than the increase required for it to enter awareness.

papers.title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression
papers.abstract: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.

papers.title: Cellular-resolution Three-photon Ultra-Deep Imaging (TrUDI) of neuronalpopulation activity at 2 mm depth in the mammalian brain
papers.abstract: Extending the depth reach of multi-photon microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an exponentially hard problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain. However, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which the out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal arising from suboptimal optical design and acquisition conditions. Here, we demonstrate a Three-photon Ultra-Deep Imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI optimally matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and non-linear limits for safe laser exposure. At the same time, TrUDI remains compatible with the spatial and temporal requirements for single-cell resolution calcium imaging, and its parameters are tuned to the photo-physics of 3p excitation and the scattering properties of the mouse brain tissue. Our approach results in a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photons at the same laser power as in previous approaches. We use TrUDI to demonstrate in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 x 230 um2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

papers.title: LATS2 modulates synaptic organization and function by regulating actin dynamics
papers.abstract: Recent work has highlighted the importance of core Hippo pathway kinases in cycling cells. Many of these kinases are also expressed in post-mitotic neurons, where they have been linked to synaptic function, and more recently a number have been shown to be dysregulated in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimers disease. Despite this, little is known about the specific role or subcellular localization of the Large Tumor Suppressor kinases, LATS1 and LATS2, in postmitotic neurons. Previously, we demonstrated that LATS1 plays an important role in synapse development; however, the role of LATS2 remains poorly understood. Here, we examined the distribution and function of LATS2 and found that it is highly expressed in CA3/CA4 neurons of the hippocampus and localized throughout dendrites and dendritic spines. In contrast to LATS1, LATS2 expression remains stable throughout neuronal development. Furthermore, ectopic expression of LATS2 induces kinase-dependent structural spine defects, alters actin dynamics and reduces activity-dependent synaptic SEP-GluR1 fluorescence. Collectively, these findings reveal a unique distribution LATS2 in the hippocampus and demonstrate that LATS2 directly regulates actin dynamics and GluR1-containing AMPAR trafficking.

papers.title: A new Mmrn1-CreERT2 Mouse Model for High-Fidelity Labeling of Adult Lymphatic Endothelium
papers.abstract: Cell type-specific Cre driver lines are essential for studying organ-specific biology in vivo, but recombination in unintended targets can limit their interpretive power. The dural meninges harbor a distinct network of lymphatic vessels implicated in neurological processes ranging from neurodevelopment to neurodegeneration. Current lymphatic reporters, driven by Prox1, Lyve1 or Vegfr3, efficiently recombine in lymphatic endothelial cells, including in the dura, but are also expressed in other CNS cell populations, resulting in non-lymphatic recombination that complicates interpretation. Here, we identify Mmrn1 as a gene specifically enriched in lymphatic endothelial cells throughout the body, with no detectable expression in other CNS cells. We generated an Mmrn1CreERT2 mouse line and show that, in adult mice, it drives recombination restricted to lymphatic endothelial cells, with no detectable recombination in non-lymphatic CNS populations. A similar but less complete recombination is observed in developing mice. This tool offers the lymphatic field a new means to specifically manipulate lymphatic vasculature and study its cell-specific functions.

papers.title: A Relational Code for Objects in Primate Frontal Cortex
papers.abstract: When we remember a scene, we recall both the locations of individual objects and their spatial arrangement. Yet, how neurons encode this arrangement alongside individual locations is unknown. In this work, we recorded large-scale neural activity from the frontal and supplementary eye fields of monkeys performing a two-object spatial working-memory task. Using a continuum of two object configurations, we tested whether neurons encoded individual object locations or the spatial relationship between them. Many neurons had well-defined position tuning when a single object was presented. With two objects, responses spanned a continuum from retinotopic to relational tuning. Surprisingly, most units were better explained by relational tuning than retinotopic tuning. Relational and retinotopic units encoded complementary dimensions of the stimulus, and their observed mixture supported near-optimal population decoding of object locations. Relational tuning was systematically aligned with single-object receptive fields, enabling a readout that produced repulsive biases resembling those observed in behavior. Standard multi-object models such as averaging and normalization failed to reproduce the observed continuum, whereas a model integrating receptive fields over potential saccades captured it. These findings show that the frontal oculomotor cortex represents not only where objects are, but also how they are arranged with respect to one another.

papers.title: Hidden Markov Modeling Reveals Altered Functional Network Dynamics in Multiple Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Purpose: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a neurodegenerative and demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. Recent evidence suggests that localized gray matter atrophy in MS may be involved in distributed functional brain networks. However, the dynamic trajectory of functional network alterations in MS remains unclear. The current study extends prior network-mediated findings and aims to investigate the dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) and energetic landscape across an atrophy-prone network in MS. Methods: Twenty MS participants and twenty healthy controls (HC) underwent resting-state fMRI. The atrophy-based functional network (AFN) model was implemented, and time series from atrophy-prone regions were fit to a 12-state hidden Markov model. Each functional network state, a recurring pattern of activity across the AFN, was characterized by the AFN regions with the strongest activation. The states were then grouped into two metastates. Dynamic functional network metrics were compared between groups by permutation testing and correlated with disability and cognition. The energetic landscape of the network was mapped with a pairwise maximum-entropy model. Temporal irreversibility was also measured, which defines the arrow-of-time asymmetry of network dynamics. Results: People with MS showed lower occupancy of state 1, which peaked on the right middle frontal and anterior cingulate cortex. Occupancy and mean lifetime were higher in states 3 and 10 (p < 0.05). In state 3, cortical activity was below the network average, and state 10 peaked on the postcentral gyrus. At the metastate level, MS participants spent more time in metastate M1 and less in M2 (p = 0.04). Within the MS group, a longer interval between visits to state 3 was associated with greater disability (r = 0.57), and a higher switching rate in state 10 with poorer verbal fluency (r = -0.50). The energetic landscape was similar between groups. Temporal irreversibility was lower in MS, mainly across subcortical connections. Conclusion: MS participants dwelled longer in specific dFC states of the AFN, while the rate of transition between states did not differ from healthy controls. Dynamic functional network metrics were associated with disability and cognitive performance and may serve as functional correlates of clinical impairment. The states were similar between groups, whereas the directed drive between states was lower across subcortical connections. This pattern suggests altered network dynamics rather than altered network architecture in MS. Findings from this study characterize the functional network dynamics of neurodegeneration in MS, which may inform future development of network-based approaches for monitoring disease progression.

papers.title: Responses to unannounced rule changes in adults with developmental disabilities: A community-based pilot study with consumer-grade EEG
papers.abstract: Unannounced changes in rules or environments often precede challenging behavior and limit community participation for adults with developmental disabilities, yet their responses to change have rarely been quantified directly. We recruited adults with developmental disabilities, including those with intellectual disability, at a community day-service center. We administered a probabilistic reversal learning task and recorded resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) via a 14-channel wireless EEG system. Among the 12 adults who performed the task, total errors were comparable across participants (range 31-57), whereas a switch bias index, contrasting perseverative errors (persisting with the previously correct option) with regressive errors (failing to maintain the newly correct option), ranged from -0.96 to +0.91. In the 9 participants included in resting-state EEG analyses, a flatter aperiodic spectrum over the frontal cluster (preregistered, but selected as the focus post hoc) was associated with fewer switches after negative feedback ({rho} = .80) and more perseverative errors ({rho} = -.72). The preregistered parieto-occipital cluster showed the same direction ({rho} = .69, 95% confidence interval [-.11, .97], n = 8), which was opposite to the preregistered prediction. Frontal alpha peak amplitude was associated with accuracy ({rho} = .77), and the between-run reliability of resting-state measures was .82-.99. These findings provide preliminary evidence that EEG recorded in community settings can capture individual differences in how people respond to change. Field measurement that includes people with intellectual disability may help extend the evidence base for the Sustainable Development Goals of good health and well-being (SDG 3) and reduced inequalities (SDG 10).

papers.title: The Alzheimer's disease risk gene ABCA7 regulates microglial lysosomal and lipid homeostasis and promotes phagocytosis to maintain neuronal health
papers.abstract: Background: Loss of function mutations in the lipid transporter ABCA7 have been linked to increased risk for late onset Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although rare and common variants in ABCA7 associated with AD alter the coding sequence and are predicted to impair protein function, the precise cell-type consequences of ABCA7 deficiency remain incompletely defined. Methods: We used CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) that were deficient for ABCA7 (ABCA7-KO) and their wild-type (ABCA7-WT) isogenic counterparts and subsequently performed unbiased proteomics on differentiated astrocytes (iAs), neurons (iNs) and microglia (iMGs). ABCA7 deficiency in iMGs produced the largest proteomic changes, so we therefore conducted additional functional analyses to define its effects on microglial lysosomal activity, phagocytosis, and lipid metabolism. In addition, we leveraged CRISPR/Cas9 to correct the ABCA7 rs3752246 AD risk variant in patient-derived iPSCs and compared proteomic and functional phenotypes between corrected iMGs and isogenic mutant carriers. Finally, we examined the functional consequence of ABCA7-deficient microglia on neurons. Results: ABCA7-KO iMGs were deficient for proteins involved in lysosome function, measured by down-regulated lysosomal proteomic signatures, as well as reduced DQ-BSA activity and reduced LAMP1+ area. Additionally, ABCA7-KO iMGs displayed impaired phagocytic capacity and increased inflammatory markers, including MHC proteins CD1A and CD1E, and IL-18. Multi-omic integration of lipidomic and proteomic profiles nominated a dysregulated metabolic network characterized by altered phospholipid steady-state metabolism and increased lipid peroxidation in ABCA7-KO iMGs. This was complemented by an accumulation of polyunsaturated triacylglycerols and lipid droplets, suggesting that ABCA7 deficiency disrupts intracellular lipid dynamics. This was supported by the alleviation of lysosomal and lipid droplet phenotypes through the inhibiting the synthesis of triacylglycerols. Concordantly, proteomic and functional analyses revealed lysosomal dysfunction in rs3752246-mutant iMGs, suggesting a shared ABCA7-dependent mechanism underlying AD risk. Tri-cultures of iNs, iAs and iMGs revealed that ABCA7 deficiency in iMGs worsened AD-relevant neuronal measures such as tau phosphorylation and synapse number. Conclusions: This work supplies evidence for the important role of ABCA7 in microglia and provides unique insights into the molecular and functional consequences of reduced ABCA7 function in lysosomal and lipid regulation, paving a path forward to a more comprehensive understanding of AD molecular subtypes and personalized therapeutics.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Theory Unifying Value and Schema in the Prefrontal Cortex
papers.abstract: Animals exhibit behavioural flexibility by making reward-optimal decisions in unfamiliar situations. Computing value from minimal reward feedback requires leveraging known structure in the world. The Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) plays a pivotal role in both value computation and learning world structure, however mechanistic explanations for each---within the frameworks of Reinforcement Learning and Cognitive Maps---are largely distinct. We develop a mechanistic model of PFC that unifies value and structure through behavioural flexibility. In this model, value acts as a control signal that gates structured working memory representations of the current context in order to ultimately control behaviour. This is a significant departure from the conventional perspective of value, in which it is used for action readout. Critically, this model generalises to novel contexts without the need for additional synaptic plasticity. We demonstrate that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) meta-trained with either reinforcement learning or supervised learning recapitulate this exact model on various value-based tasks. These results not only provide a parsimonious explanation of both the value and schema frameworks of PFC function, but also propose a new mechanistic interpretation of the role of PFC in flexible decision making.

papers.title: Three-dimensional object-based quantification of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit colocalization using Imaris
papers.abstract: Neural circuit function depends not only on synaptic connectivity but also on the molecular composition and spatial organization of neurotransmitter receptors. Determining whether receptor subunits occupy shared or distinct domains requires spatial measurements capable of resolving sparse receptor puncta across neural tissue and, when needed, restricting analysis to defined cellular compartments. Conventional intensity-based colocalization metrics can be difficult to interpret for sparse, punctate signals and do not inherently provide object-level classification or cell-specific analysis. Here, we describe a three-dimensional object-based colocalization workflow for endogenously tagged nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) subunits imaged by Airyscan super-resolution confocal microscopy and analyzed in Imaris. Individual receptor puncta are segmented as 3D surface objects and classified as colocalized or non-colocalized using a control-defined spatial overlap criterion. The workflow supports analysis within a defined region of the ventral nerve cord neuropil or within genetically labeled motor-neuron dendritic compartments. For dendrite-restricted analysis, receptor puncta are first selected by their overlap with the dendritic surface before receptor-receptor overlap is quantified. The overlap criterion is empirically calibrated using positive and negative biological controls processed under the same imaging and analysis conditions, providing a reproducible alternative to arbitrary threshold selection. This approach enables receptor organization to be quantified within the neuropil and genetically labeled motor-neuron dendritic compartments and can be adapted to other epitope-tagged receptors, ion channels, and synaptic proteins.

papers.title: Oxytocin modulates behavioral economic and dopaminergic measures of motivation to seek intravenous oxycodone in rats
papers.abstract: The opioid epidemic persists despite available pharmacotherapies for opioid use disorder (OUD), motivating interest in treatments targeting the motivational and neurochemical substrates of opioid seeking. Peripherally administered oxytocin (OT) attenuates drug seeking and consumption across substances and modulates the mesolimbic dopamine system, yet its effects on opioid seeking and its underlying neurobiology remain poorly characterized. Here we investigated the effects of OT on behavioral and dopaminergic measures of opioid reinforcement using in vivo fiber photometry with the dopamine sensor, GRABDA2m, in the nucleus accumbens (NA) core of male and female rats. Daily OT (15 IU/kg, IP) administered 30 min prior to operant sessions increased demand elasticity for intravenous oxycodone self-administration in males but not females. Acute OT (15 and 45 IU/kg, IP) increased GRABDA2m dopamine signal in the NA core in females, and potentiated oxycodone-evoked dopamine release in both sexes. In a high-effort task, NA core dopamine increased prior to lever presses, and acute OT (15 IU/kg, IP) produced sex-divergent effects on phasic NA core dopamine release during lever pressing, increasing peak signal and area under the curve measures in males. Support vector machine classifiers determined that features of dopamine transients (e.g., mean peak, standard deviation of the amplitude, peak-valley range) before an active lever press distinguished between treatment and sex. Thus, the ability of chronic oxytocin to reduce the motivation to self-administer oxycodone in male rats is independent of oxycodone-induced NA dopamine release but rather may involve dopamine transmission during lever pressing under high effort conditions.

papers.title: Temporal modulation of cortical parvalbumin and somatostatin neurons shapes network activation and adaptation during microstimulation
papers.abstract: Parvalbumin-positive (PV) and somatostatin-positive (SOM) inhibitory interneurons play distinct and critical roles in cortical sensory processing, yet their activation dynamics during patterned input remain unclear. This study used two-photon calcium imaging to measure how PV and SOM interneurons are activated and regulate layer 2/3 somatosensory cortical activity during prolonged, patterned input with 22 clinically relevant microstimulation patterns divided by temporal pattern (fixed, burst, or dynamic/biomimetic) and amplitude. Activation over time depended on the interaction between microstimulation amplitude, frequency, and duration. For fixed-frequency stimulation, PV neurons were generally more strongly activated than unlabeled neurons, while SOM neurons were more strongly engaged at higher amplitudes and frequencies, corresponding with greater suppression of surrounding populations over time. Burst patterns limited suppression by evoking stronger and more sustained activation than fixed-frequency patterns especially in PV neurons, potentially by reducing SOM feedback. Theta-burst stimulation (TBS) strongly activated and facilitated SOM neurons, which may underlie its therapeutic effects. Dynamic amplitude modulation preserved excitatory-inhibitory balance by eliciting brief, consistent responses that resemble natural sensory input while reducing long-term adaptation. Many findings fit a model in which PV provides fast-adapting feedforward inhibition and SOM provides slower-facilitating feedback. Supporting this model, distant PV neurons reached peak activation earlier than non-PV neurons, and SOM neurons later than non-SOM neurons during stimulation bursts. A simple computational model built on these dynamics reproduced observed responses, including distance-related effects. Neurons recruited directly bypass SOM input onto their dendrites leading to rapid PV-mediated depression but increasing activity across the stimulation pattern. Together, these results inform the design of microstimulation-based sensory restoration and clarify the circuit-level roles of PV and SOM neurons in transient and sustained inhibitory control of somatosensory cortex.

papers.title: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), estrogen receptors, and mossy cells
papers.abstract: Dentate gyrus (DG) function depends on the neurotrophin brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) which shows robust synthesis in the principal cells, the granule cells (GCs). However, BDNF protein is present in the inner molecular layer (IML), where most afferents to GCs are from hilar mossy cells (MCs). Therefore, we asked whether MCs express BDNF mRNA and protein. Using adult mice, we found that MC BDNF mRNA and protein were expressed in the majority of MC somata and few other hilar neurons. Interestingly, IML BDNF was significantly greater in the ventral compared to dorsal DG. Additionally, dorsal IML BDNF was significantly higher in females on proestrous morning, when serum levels of estrogen peak, relative to metestrous morning, when estrogen is lower. Consistent with this observation, ventral MC somata, which project to the dorsal IML, showed more BDNF mRNA on proestrous morning than metestrous morning. Next, we asked if strong IML BDNF protein expression on proestrous morning was due to estrogen action at estrogen receptors (ERs) because estrogen binding to ERs can increase BDNF synthesis. We found that MCs have high expression of all ERs: ER, ER{beta} and GPER1 in both sexes. When sexes were pooled, the percent of MCs labeled by ER{beta} and GPER1 exceeded the percent of MCs expressing ER. When proestrous females were examined, GPER1-labeled hilar cells were greater than hilar cells labeled by ER. The results demonstrate robust MC somatic expression of BDNF, relatively high ventral IML expression of BDNF, and estrous cycle dependence. The results also highlight robust MC ER expression, especially ER{beta} and GPER1, making the hilus a previously underestimated site of estrogen and BDNF action.

papers.title: Theta sequences support real-time spatial memory retrieval
papers.abstract: Oscillations play a critical role in orchestrating the timing of neural activity during cognitive processes. In the hippocampus, place cells encode spatial locations, and their activity is organized by theta oscillations into sequences that represent past, present, and potential future states. Recently, scrambling theta oscillations in vivo was shown to impair memory retrieval during navigation and decision-making, while leaving place cell activity intact. This surprising result highlights that the exact mechanisms underlying real-time memory encoding and retrieval in the hippocampus remain undefined. Here, we use a spiking neural network model of hippocampal theta sequences to evaluate the consequences of theta frequency scrambling on both representational learning and real-time spatial memory retrieval. We first show that frequency scrambling disrupts theta sequences and phase precession. Specifically, increased frequency scrambling was associated with a gradually degraded relationship between theta phase and spike timing, and ultimately abolished the predictive nature of place fields. When hippocampal spikes are required to solve a T-maze alternation task, the number of successful trials and navigation efficiency decreased with increasing values of frequency scrambling. These results could advance our understanding of how theta modulated neural activity supports memory-guided decision-making in real time and demonstrate why navigation fails when disrupting theta, despite intact spatial representations.

papers.title: Long-Range Glutamatergic Projections Target Hippocampal Cajal-Retzius Cells Through Atypical Receptor Signaling
papers.abstract: Cajal-Retzius (CR) cells are a population of early-born, transient neurons that serve an indispensable role during embryonic brain development. Postnatally, most CR cells undergo programmed cell-death, except in a few areas, including the hippocampus, where they persist until adulthood. The hippocampal population of CR (hCR) cells have previously been implicated in receiving and facilitating ingrowth of entorhinal afferents and the establishment of the hippocampal circuit. Nevertheless, only local GABAergic synaptic input has been demonstrated onto hCR cells before. Through transsynaptic rabies tracing we show that hCR cells receive input for at least seven extrahippocampal areas, all putative glutamatergic populations, even though CR cell spontaneous activity is speculated to be exclusively mediated through GABAergic action. Here, we show that a portion of CR cell spontaneous activity is strychnine-sensitive, and that glutamatergic fibers from entorhinal cortex layer II apposition themselves in physiological distance (<300 nm) to glycinergic receptors on hCR cells. We propose that hCR cells guide several, if not all, afferents terminating in stratum lacunosum moleculare and the outer molecular layer in the hippocampus. These findings shine new light on how hCR cells might facilitate hippocampal maturation.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal transcriptomic dynamic across the auditory pathway from young to old age in 5xFAD Alzheimer disease mice
papers.abstract: Auditory dysfunction can precede clinical dementia, but the molecular progression of Alzheimer disease (AD) pathology from the sensory periphery to auditory cortex remains poorly resolved. We performed bulk RNA sequencing of auditory cortex (AC), inferior colliculus (IC), cochlear nucleus (CN), and cochlea from 5xFAD and wild-type mice at postnatal day 50 (P50), 8 months, 11 months, and 16 months. Age-specific genotype effects and Genotype x Age interactions were evaluated using DESeq2, followed by Hallmark, KEGG, and Gene Ontology gene-set enrichment analyses and a cross-region synthesis of interaction trajectories. At P50, AC, IC, and cochlea showed coordinated suppression of mitochondrial metabolism, translation, RNA processing, and proteostasis, whereas CN displayed the opposite metabolic and biosynthetic profile together with reduced synaptic and adhesion programs. At 8 months, inflammatory interactions converged across all four regions, including interferon, complement, IL6-JAK-STAT3, and broader immune-response pathways. This coordination fractured at 11 months: AC and IC retained inflammatory and negative synaptic shifts, whereas CN and cochlea frequently changed in the opposite direction, including transient positive shifts in synaptic programs. By 16 months, immune interactions converged again, while metabolic, proteostatic, and synaptic trajectories remained region dependent; CN opposed AC, IC, and cochlea in several major metabolic programs. These findings define a distributed, asynchronous response rather than a monotonic bottom-up or top-down progression. The resulting spatiotemporal map links early metabolic stress, intermediate central-peripheral decoupling, and late inflammatory convergence, providing a molecular framework for evaluating peripheral to central auditory gain and temporal-processing measures as candidate indicators of AD progression.

papers.title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
papers.abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

papers.title: Vibrotactile stimulation on the upper back requires stronger vibration during goal-directed reaching but does not impede reaching performance
papers.abstract: Vibrotactile stimulation is a promising method of biofeedback, with potential applications for ergonomic posture and balance, rehabilitation, and motor learning. These applications require balancing tactile perception with motor performance and cognitive workload. In this study, participants performed a detection task, a reaching task, and a concurrent reach-and-detect task, with vibrotactile signals delivered on the hand or upper back. Sensitivity to stimuli, motor performance, and cognitive workload were compared for each task. Sensitivity was suppressed during movement, but this suppression was greater on hand compared to the upper back. Movement time was slowed by vibration on the hand but not the upper back. Mental workload and task complexity increased for the reach-and-detect task compared to the individual tasks. We conclude that vibrotactile feedback devices worn on the upper back do not impede motor performance, with only minor tactile suppression. This could be overcome by presenting highly salient or personalized feedback.

papers.title: Functional characterization of the 26RFa/orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamic area reveals their key role in the control of glucose homeostasis
papers.abstract: Defining the nature and molecular mechanisms of the neurocircuitry controlling glucose homeostasis is crucial in understanding how alterations in these pathways promote the development of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Here, we functionally characterize a population of lateral hypothalamic neurons co-expressing the anti-hyperglycemic neuropeptides 26RFa and orexin. Using complementary chemogenetic, pharmacological and genetic approaches, including mice deficient for 26RFa, orexin or both neuropeptides, we investigated the respective contribution of each signaling system to glucose homeostasis. We found that lateral hypothalamic 26RFa neurons extensively co-express orexin, defining a distinct peptidergic population with convergent anti-hyperglycemic properties. Unexpectedly, chemogenetic activation of these neurons potentiated glucose-induced hyperglycemia despite the anti-hyperglycemic properties of both neuropeptides. To understand this paradox, we examined the transcriptional responses of the 26RFa and orexin peptidergic systems and found that neuronal activation was associated with coordinated, glycemic state-dependent downregulation of both signaling systems. Furthermore, genetic loss-of-function approaches revealed distinct contributions of the two neuropeptidergic systems, with orexin signaling mediating most of the metabolic consequences of neuronal activation, whereas 26RFa signaling is required for the dynamic regulation of orexin expression. Finally, our findings provide new insights into the functional organization of lateral hypothalamic 26RFa/orexin neurons and advance our understanding of how coordinated neuropeptidergic signaling contributes to systemic glucose homeostasis.

papers.title: Diurnal Variations in the Cholinergic System of the Nucleus Accumbens
papers.abstract: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) plays a critical role in reward-related behaviors, which exhibit diurnal variations. Cholinergic interneurons (CINs) are the primary source of acetylcholine within the NAc and regulate local dopamine (DA) signaling through nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs). Although there are diurnal variations in NAc dynamics, little is known about whether CIN activity and nicotinic signaling also vary across the light/dark cycle. Here, we aimed to determine diurnal variations in the NAc cholinergic system using ex vivo fast-scan cyclic voltammetry and cell-attached electrophysiological recordings in male rodents. We examined time-of-day-dependent differences in nAChR-mediated modulation of DA release, spontaneous CIN firing frequency, and firing patterns. We found that spontaneous CIN firing varied across the light/dark cycle, with increased activity during the dark cycle. Additionally, bath application of nicotine (NIC), mecamylamine (MEC), and dihydro-{beta}-erythroidine (DH{beta}E) reduced CIN firing frequency during the dark cycle, with only MEC decreasing firing frequency in the light cycle. NIC and MEC also altered CIN firing patterns during the dark cycle, whereas DH{beta}E primarily affected firing frequency. Together, these findings demonstrate diurnal variations in NAc CIN activity and reveal time-of-day-dependent differences in the effects of nAChR modulation on spontaneous firing. These results suggest that nicotinic signaling may contribute to diurnal regulation of NAc cholinergic activity, providing insight into mechanisms underlying time-of-day-dependent changes in reward circuitry.

papers.title: Sex shapes capillary flows and oxygen extraction in the middle-aged mouse brain
papers.abstract: Sex differences in brain aging are well documented, but their origin within the cerebrovascular hierarchy remains unclear. Here we show that cortical blood flow is higher in female than male mice at 15 months of age, at a point when an earlier sex difference in pulsatility and resistance indices has already converged, pial vessel diameter shows no difference between sexes, and estrogen levels are similar between sexes. Using an indicator-dilution and intravascular oxygen measurements using two-photon microscopy, we found that capillary transit-time heterogeneity (CTH) scales more steeply with mean transit time in females, consistent with a passively regulated capillary network, and that this is accompanied by reduced oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) without deficit in arterial oxygen delivery. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that sex differences are organized into distinct regional programs, most prominently in white matter, where a male-associated myelin and axonogenesis signature accompanies reduced white matter volume in females. These molecular and structural differences coincide with elevated hippocampal microglial reactivity and an altered spatial search strategy in females, without any detectable differences in circulating markers of stress, blood-brain barrier integrity, or immunity. Together, these findings indicate that sex differences in the aging brain are expressed at the level of capillary flow regulation and regional tissue programs rather than through bulk cerebral blood flow alone, and that elevated blood flow in females can mask, rather than reflect, adequate tissue oxygenation.

papers.title: Temporal tuning of actin nucleation by the repurposed DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 encodes distinct axon guidance decisions
papers.abstract: Axon guidance is essential for neural circuit assembly and function. While much of the repertoire of guidance cues and receptors is known, its limited diversity cannot fully explain the remarkable complexity of the brain connectome. How temporally ordered, context-dependent intrinsic programs shape the diversity of axonal responses to guidance signals remains poorly understood. We reveal how non-canonical Wnt5a signalling repurposes the DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 as a downstream integrator to control retinal ganglion cell axon decision-making at the midline. We demonstrate that differential RAD51/fignl1 expression and interaction dynamics between ipsilateral and contralateral axons tunes the magnitude and temporal dynamics of F-actin nucleation, thereby encoding their trajectory choice. Our findings establish temporal control of cytoskeletal dynamics as a key determinant of axon decision-making and thereby a fundamental layer of circuit wiring. They provide a potential mechanistic framework linking mutations in the DNA repair gene RAD51 to neurodevelopmental disorders with midline guidance defects.

papers.title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
papers.abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory. Net excitatory input onto this population decreased, most strongly that from older-memory populations, which allowed inputs of older memories to drive their own neurons again. Spreading the same total synaptic change evenly across all target populations abolished this recovery. We call this mechanism reactivation-targeted pruning: plasticity is confined to one population, whose neurons lose inputs that are silent when they fire. The mechanism held under Dale's law, and depression of excitatory synapses alone, without any inhibitory plasticity, was sufficient. These findings suggest mechanistic principles underlying REM sleep's role in memory consolidation and highlight the potential for integrating human-like learning behaviors into artificial neural networks.

papers.title: Adolescent prodromal phenotypes of psychiatric disorders: insights from a novel DISC1-perturbed monkey model
papers.abstract: Neurodevelopmental deficits frequently lead to mild but significant adolescent social and cognitive changes, representing prodromal manifestations of adult-onset psychiatric disorders in a cross-disease manner. Although experimental medicine utilizes animal models to address the mechanisms, rodent brains lack critical structures for human higher brain functions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. To fill this translational gap, we generated monkeys with an impaired DISC1 gene locus, targeting the multifunctional protein essential for neurodevelopment and involved in transdiagnostic mental health risks. Here we analyze the F0 animals by minimizing mosaicism. At ages equivalent to human adolescence, these monkeys exhibited blunted responsiveness to social stimuli and increased internal drives, mirroring altered social behaviors in the prodromal stage in humans. Resting-state functional MRI data indicated disrupted global functional connectivity and reorganization of network topology, marked by a shift in the dominance of brain hubs from prefrontal regions to sensory areas. This primate model provides a unique platform for studying psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia, across the developmental trajectory.

papers.title: Real-Time Neurotransmitter Sensing in Midbrain Organoids Using 3D Carbon Cup Electrodes
papers.abstract: Real time, chemically selective detection of neurotransmitter release in brain organoids remains a challenge due to their complex three dimensional architecture and limited optical accessibility. We introduce 3D printed carbon cup electrodes (CCEs) -pyrolyzed, multi level pillar structures - designed to confine a single organoid, increase electroactive surface area, and enable amperometric recordings of oxidizable neurotransmitters. The CCEs exhibit excellent electrochemical performance and reproducibility, supporting diffusion controlled dopamine redox behavior without interference from culture medium. Using ventral midbrain (vMB) organoids at two maturation stages (Day 30 and Day 90), we demonstrate real time detection of potassium evoked dopamine release directly from organoids. Mature organoids exhibit higher peak currents, correlating with increased tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression confirmed by immunocytochemistry. Embedding organoids in Matrigel significantly attenuates dopamine signals, indicating a diffusion barrier that limits stimulant access and/or dopamine transport to the electrode. Repetitive stimulations reveal progressive depletion of dopamine stores, consistent with diminished vesicular release. Chemical perturbations using 6 hydroxydopamine and verapamil further validate the platform by producing substantial reductions in dopamine release accompanied by loss of TH neurons. These results establish CCEs as a powerful tool for label free, real-time monitoring of neurotransmission in human organoids, with potential for multiplexed sensing and integration of enzymatic detection strategies for non electroactive neurotransmitters.

papers.title: LIF is a pro-algesic mediator in human and mouse models of arthritis-related pain
papers.abstract: Purpose: Emerging clinical and experimental data suggest that JAK inhibitors (JAKi) are effective in reducing pain in Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). We recently showed that JAK/STAT signalling cytokines, specifically IL-6, LIF and IL-11, are present in the RA joint and can act directly on human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived sensory neurons by increasing their STAT3 phosphorylation (pSTAT3) levels and expression of select pain-relevant genes. In this study, we determined that LIF is the most consequential cytokine out of the three, altering neuronal signalling, outgrowth and pain-like behaviours in in vitro and in vivo models of arthritis. Methods: Human iPSC-derived sensory neurons were stimulated with RA synovial fluid (SF) or with cytokine-treated RA synovial fibroblast conditioned media (CM) in the absence or presence of anti-cytokine antibodies. pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 levels, and gene expression patterns, were assessed by Western blot and RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq). The immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6) was assessed for LIF-induced JAK/STAT signalling in addition to neurite outgrowth assays as a functional readout of the sensory neurons. Lastly, mouse models were used to assess pain-related behaviours in vivo. Results: LIF was found to be consistently present in the SF from painful joints from individuals with inflammatory arthritis. Western blotting revealed that the addition of RA SF to iPSC-derived sensory neurons led to LIF-dependent induction of pSTAT3 and pSTAT1, while RNA-seq demonstrated that LIF alters the transcriptome of sensory neurons more prominently than IL-6 and IL-11, up-regulating signature genes related to peripheral neuron sensitization, such as TRPV1, NTRK1, BDNF, HRH1 and SCN10A. Similarly, cytokine-treated fibroblast conditioned media was shown to induce neuronal pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 and upregulate expression of BDNF, HRH1 and VGF in a LIF-dependent manner. Additionally, the immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6), which also exhibited LIF-induced pSTAT1 and pSTAT3, showed increased neurite outgrowth after axotomy when treated with LIF. Finally, in a mouse model of inflammatory arthritis, LIF was shown to be significantly increased in the affected joint. Furthermore, intraarticular injection of LIF into a healthy mouse knee resulted in increased responsiveness to painful pressure stimuli in that joint. Conclusions: Our data indicate that LIF may be a pro-algesic mediator and a possible therapeutic target to improve pain management in individuals living with inflammatory arthritis.

papers.title: Exposure to childhood adversity and adult alcohol, nicotine, and illicit drug use in Germany: a cross-sectional analysis of the German National Cohort (NAKO)
papers.abstract: Rationale: Exposure to adversity in childhood and adolescence (i.e., "early-life stress"; ELS) is a well-established risk factor for substance use. Objectives: The aim of this study was to investigate associations between ELS exposure and substance use across subtypes of ELS, different substance classes, and behavioral profiles of substance use. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we examined associations between ELS exposure and substance use in a population-based sample of 172,173 adults aged 19-74 years from the German National Cohort (NAKO). ELS exposure was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Screener. Substance use included nicotine, alcohol, and illicit drug use. Associations were examined using regression models evaluating overall ELS exposure, cumulative trauma load, and ELS subtypes. Latent class analysis (LCA) was conducted to identify substance use profiles. Results: ELS exposure was associated with higher odds of smoking, greater smoking severity, heavier alcohol consumption among drinkers, and higher odds of lifetime illicit drug use. Overall, the strongest associations were observed for opioid and stimulant use. Dose-response analyses revealed higher risk with increasing numbers of ELS subtypes. Abuse-related subtypes, particularly exposure to physical and sexual abuse, consistently showed strongest independent associations across substances, whereas neglect exhibited weaker, more variable associations. LCA identified four substance use profiles, with ELS exposure predicting membership in more severe polysubstance classes. Conclusions: ELS emerged as a robust risk factor for adult substance use, underscoring the need for trauma-informed approaches in clinical practice, public health, and policy to mitigate the long-term consequences of early adversity.

papers.title: Cooperative processing of visual threat across collicular pathways
papers.abstract: Rapid defensive actions require the transformation of sensory cues into appropriate motor responses. The superior colliculus is central to this transformation, containing defined cell-types that form parallel output pathways linking visual inputs to distinct behaviors. However, whether these pathways act independently or cooperate remains unclear. Here we combine cell-type-specific inhibition, large-scale electrophysiology, and functional ultrasound imaging to determine how these pathways contribute to visually evoked defensive behaviors. Inhibiting either narrow-field or wide-field neurons impaired escape to overhead visual threats, demonstrating that both pathways contribute to escape. Recordings from downstream targets revealed a compact representation in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus that selectively distinguished visual stimuli associated with escape, whereas the lateral posterior thalamus contained a broader representation of visual stimuli. The representation of visual threat in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus predicted escape initiation and vigor in freely moving animals. Across the brain, functional ultrasound imaging showed that visual stimuli recruited distinct patterns of activity that could not be explained by response magnitude alone or by the contribution of single cell-types. Together, these results reveal a cooperative circuit architecture in which parallel pathways carry distinct but complementary signals that jointly support visually evoked escape.

papers.title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
papers.abstract: The human brain is remarkably dynamic, continuously adapting to internal and external signals across rapid and protracted timescales. While both male and female brains are influenced by sex hormones to drive adaptive behavioural and physiological changes, the ovarian cycle in female mammals represents a conserved naturalistic model to understand how hormones such as estradiol (E2) alter cellular and network states to shape brain function. To understand whether and how the ovarian cycle influences sensory cortical processing, we investigated cortical network activity at rest and upon auditory stimulation across the ovarian cycle in mice and human subjects. We recorded EEG activity in men and women and intracortical local field potentials in male and female mice. Female participants were tested during two phases of their ovarian cycle characterized by low E2 levels (early follicular phase in women; late estrus in mice) and high E2 levels (late follicular phase in women; proestrus in mice). Across species, high endogenous or exogenous estradiol was associated with a steeper aperiodic power spectral slope, indicating decreased excitatory/inhibitory drive and attenuated auditory entrainment following a 40Hz stimulation. At the single-cell level, high E2 selectively increased the baseline and sustained 40-Hz firing of putative fast-spiking interneurons while reducing their temporal coherence during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity, suggesting that E2 enhances inhibitory tone, while disrupting the temporal coordination of inhibitory networks. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that estradiol dynamically modulates cortical network states and auditory responsiveness. This underscores the necessity of investigating hormone-brain coupling as an evolutionarily conserved model essential for yielding translational insights into sex-specific neurobiology.
